findings.rule: source check; brief A (no generalization beyond the population studied)
findings.issue: The abstinence range of 5 days to 3 weeks 'in most studies' is the Ashok abstract's description of all 31 studies in the review, not of the 9 amphetamine-type transporter studies. Those 9 (refs 27–35) include McCann 1998, Johanson 2006 and McCann 2008, whose groups were abstinent for years on average, and the claim's own PET studies had group means of about 2 months to about 6 years.
findings.evidence: ashok_2017: Abstract › Results, 1st sentence (introduces the results for every outcome); Results › Dopamine transporter, 1st paragraph cites refs 27–35 for the 9 studies; reference list: ref 28 Johanson 2006, 29 McCann 2008, 30 McCann 1998, 33 Volkow 2001b. hart_2012 p. 593, Table 2: Johanson mean 3.4 years; McCann 2008 imaging subset mean 77 months; McCann 1998 range 4–65 months. volkow_2001b p. 9416: short-abstinence group 64 days. The card sc_ashok_2017 (sample.selection_effects) draws the same wrong inference.
findings.proposed: population: 'Adults with a history of heavy methamphetamine use, abstinent for days to years (group means from about 2 months to about 6 years in the individual PET studies)'. evidence[5].extracted: '9 studies of people who used amphetamine-type stimulants (108 vs 126 controls): g −1.47 (95% CI −1.83 to −1.10), p<0.001. The abstract's statement that abstinence lasted 5 days to 3 weeks in most studies describes all 31 studies in the review; the 9 transporter studies (refs 27–35) include three whose groups were abstinent for years on average (McCann et al., 1998, 2008; Johanson et al., 2006).' Correct the same sentence in sc_ashok_2017 sample.selection_effects.

findings.rule: brief A (qualifying finding in the same source left out); brief E (other drug use)
findings.issue: Hart et al. (2012) p. 592, already anchored for McCann 1998, also describes Sekine et al. (2001): an independent Japanese group studied 11 people who used methamphetamine without other illicit drug histories and found striatal DAT about 20% lower than in 9 matched controls. The plain text names other drug use as a difference between groups but omits the one study that addressed it.
findings.evidence: hart_2012 p. 592, 'PET studies investigating DAT…', 2nd paragraph (Sekine et al., 2001, about 20% lower; reviewers note the result is not attributable to other illicit drug use); p. 593 Table 2, Sekine row (abstinence 7 days to 1.5 years).
findings.proposed: statement: after 'about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies' insert '(about 20% lower in a Japanese study of 11 people without other illicit drug use, as described by Hart et al., 2012)'. plain: replace 'They also smoked tobacco and used other drugs more often.' with 'They also smoked tobacco and used other drugs more often, though one study of people who had not used other illegal drugs found a similar difference.' New anchor: reference hart_2012, study_card sc_hart_2012, page 'p. 592', locator 'PET studies investigating DAT…, 2nd paragraph', extracted 'Sekine et al. (2001): 11 people who used methamphetamine and had no history of other illicit drug use vs 9 matched controls; striatal DAT binding about 20% lower, as described by the reviewers.', role 'supports'.

findings.rule: METHODS §6.3 (rate the claim as worded)
findings.issue: The claim is worded with magnitudes (13–28%, g −1.47) but the displayed rating (low, no downgrades although study-level risk of bias is high) applies only to the direction; the reasoning itself calls the size very low certainty. A reader sees 'low' next to the numbers.
findings.evidence: grade.reasoning ('Rated for the direction…'; size 'very low certainty'); grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note; cards sc_volkow_2001a and sc_mccann_1998 (ROBINS-E overall high), sc_ashok_2017 (AMSTAR 2 critically low).
findings.proposed: statement: replace 'The direction is consistent across research groups; the size is uncertain.' with 'The direction is consistent across research groups (certainty low); the size of the difference is very uncertain (certainty very low), because every primary study is an unadjusted comparison and the pooled estimate comes from a critically low-confidence meta-analysis.' grade.reasoning: add 'The displayed certainty applies to the direction only; for the size, a strict reading gives very low.'

findings.rule: METHODS §9 (person-first language); changelog 0.3.1 states the wording was changed
findings.issue: The displayed reasoning still says 'selected heavy users'.
findings.evidence: grade.reasoning, 2nd sentence.
findings.proposed: Replace '(selected heavy users from treatment programmes compared with advertisement-recruited controls,' with '(people with heavy use selected from treatment programmes compared with advertisement-recruited controls,'. Note: 58 anchor texts across these 11 claims still say 'users'; if anchors are displayed, the language pass should cover them too.

findings.rule: brief F (same fact with different numbers in two claims)
findings.issue: This anchor gives the short-abstinence caudate difference as 26% (the text value); the recovery claim uses 25% (Table 1) and notes the discrepancy. Both are in the source, but the two claims should show the same pair.
findings.proposed: 'In the same research programme (overlapping sample, not an independent replication), people in short abstinence (n=12) were 26% (caudate; 25.0% from Table 1) and 21% (putamen) below controls (n=11).'

findings.rule: source check (saved source with a different range)
findings.issue: London et al. (2015), a saved source cited elsewhere in section 4, gives DAT deficits of 11–28% across six PET studies, including Johanson et al. (2006), whose DAT value the claim reports only combined with VMAT2 (10–16%). The lower bound of the PET range may be 11% rather than 13%.
findings.evidence: london_2015 Molecular Imaging of Methamphetamine Users › Monoamine systems, 2nd paragraph (deficits of 11–28%; Johanson 2006, McCann 1998, 2008, Sekine 2001, Volkow 2001b, 2001d).
findings.proposed: statement: replace 'about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies (a further study reports DAT and VMAT2 together as 10–16% lower)' with 'about 13–28% lower in individual PET studies (a review gives 11–28% across six PET studies, including one described elsewhere as 10–16% lower for DAT and VMAT2 together)', with a london_2015 anchor at the stated paragraph, until Johanson et al. (2006) is read.

findings.rule: brief A (content of plain supported by the claim's anchors)
findings.issue: The plain says the groups smoked tobacco more often, but no anchor of this claim gives smoking data. The data exist in the metabolism paper on the same 15 people.
findings.evidence: volkow_2001c p. 383 (the same 15 people and 18 of the 21 controls also had the transporter scan), p. 387 (smokers 73% vs 24%); hart_2012 p. 598 (in most PET studies the methamphetamine groups reported extensive other drug use, comparison groups little).
findings.proposed: Add anchors: volkow_2001c, pp. 383, 387, 'Introduction, last paragraph; Discussion, limitations paragraph', extracted 'The 15 people in the transporter study (and 18 of 21 controls) are those of the metabolism study, in which 73% of the methamphetamine group and 24% of controls smoked.', role 'qualifies'; hart_2012, p. 598, 'Main text, 1st paragraph', extracted 'In most PET studies the methamphetamine groups reported extensive use of other drugs and comparison groups little.', role 'qualifies'.

findings.rule: brief A (qualifying finding in the same source)
findings.issue: The anchor says no heterogeneity statistics are printed, which is true, but the review's Limitations state that heterogeneity was low in every analysis except the transporter one; this supports the statement's caution about the pooled interval and is not shown.
findings.evidence: ashok_2017 Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph.
findings.proposed: evidence[6].extracted: replace 'no heterogeneity statistics are printed in the main text' with 'no heterogeneity statistics are printed in the main text, though the Limitations say heterogeneity was low in all analyses except the transporter analysis'. statement: after 'so its interval is probably too narrow' add '; the review also reports that heterogeneity was not low for the transporter analysis'.

findings.rule: brief A (editors' calculation reproduces); GRADE imprecision reasoning
findings.issue: Recomputed from Table 1, the protracted-versus-control intervals are g −0.31 (−1.17 to 0.55) in the caudate and −0.57 (−1.45 to 0.30) in the putamen, while short abstinence gives g about −1.54 and −1.51. A difference as large as in short abstinence is therefore excluded in the caudate and only just excluded in the putamen; the magnitude ('is not excluded') and the reasoning ('includes a difference as large as in short abstinence') overstate the imprecision.
findings.evidence: volkow_2001b p. 9416, Table 1: controls 1.76 (0.27) and 1.97 (0.21), n=11; short abstinence 1.32 (0.28) and 1.56 (0.30), n=12; protracted 1.67 (0.29) and 1.80 (0.35), n=10. Hedges' g with pooled SD and large-sample standard error.
findings.proposed: magnitude: replace '(n=10 vs 11; editors' calculation: g −0.3, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.6, and −0.6, −1.5 to 0.3, so a remaining difference about as large as in short abstinence, g about −1.5, is not excluded)' with '(n=10 vs 11; editors' calculation: g −0.3, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.6, and −0.6, −1.45 to 0.3, so a remaining difference of more than 1 SD is not excluded in either region; in short abstinence the differences are about −1.5 SD)'. grade.reasoning: replace 'whose interval includes a difference as large as in short abstinence' with 'whose intervals include differences of more than 1 SD (lower limits about −1.2 in the caudate and −1.45 in the putamen)'.

findings.rule: brief C (reasoning matches the domain levels); revision residue
findings.issue: The domain note still says one other PET study found no abstinence relation, while the reasoning and statement now cite three cross-sectional analyses and a SPECT follow-up that found a rise.
findings.evidence: grade.reasoning (three cross-sectional analyses); statement; changelog 0.3.0.
findings.proposed: 'Three cross-sectional analyses, one from the same programme, found no relation between time since last use and transporter levels, while a SPECT follow-up found a rise.'

findings.rule: brief A (the statement says no more than its anchors support); METHODS §4.5, §6.2
findings.issue: The statement attributes a null relation between time since last use and transporter levels to Johanson et al. (2006), as described by Hart et al. (2012), but no anchor carries it: the Hart anchor (p. 597) names only Volkow and McCann (2008), and the p. 596 anchor in the transporter claim gives Johanson's binding difference only. The source does support it, so only an anchor is missing.
findings.evidence: hart_2012 p. 596, paragraph on Johanson et al. (2006): neither imaging nor cognitive data correlated with abstinence duration; following paragraph: McCann et al. (2008) found no relation between duration of abstinence and imaging results. Card sc_hart_2012 does not record the Johanson result.
findings.proposed: Add anchor: reference hart_2012, study_card sc_hart_2012, page 'p. 596', locator 'Main text, paragraphs on Johanson et al. (2006) and McCann et al. (2008)', extracted 'Johanson et al. (2006; 16 people with methamphetamine dependence, mean abstinence 3.4 years, vs 18 controls): neither imaging nor cognitive measures correlated with abstinence duration. McCann et al. (2008): no relation between duration of abstinence and imaging results.', role 'contradicts'; and add the Johanson result to card sc_hart_2012.

findings.rule: brief B (qualifier dropped; plain contradicts a finding in the claim's own source)
findings.issue: The plain drops that no control group was rescanned, so ordinary scan-to-scan variation cannot be excluded, and omits the 2-week SPECT follow-up. It also says studies 'comparing people with shorter and longer time since last use' found no pattern, but the programme's own group comparison found higher levels in the protracted group (caudate 26% difference, p<0.01); the null results are correlations across people.
findings.evidence: volkow_2001b p. 9416 (short vs protracted groups: caudate 26% difference, p<0.01; putamen trend); volkow_2001a p. 379 (r<0.11); hart_2012 p. 596; dean_2013 p. 265 (Chou et al., 2007).
findings.proposed: 'Five people from a court-supervised treatment programme were scanned twice. After more than a year without meth, their dopamine transporter levels had risen by about a sixth to a fifth. No one who doesn't use meth was scanned twice for comparison, so ordinary variation between scans can't be ruled out. A group scanned after more than a year without meth was not clearly different from people who don't use, but the groups were too small to rule out a large difference. Three studies that looked across people for a link between time since last use and transporter levels found none. In another small study, levels rose over two weeks, but the first scan was taken while meth was still showing up in urine tests. Five people is too few to know how typical this is, and those who stayed abstinent had higher levels to begin with.'

findings.rule: brief A and E (completeness; symmetry)
findings.issue: 'The one DAT follow-up with retested controls' cannot be confirmed as the only one: two cited reviews point to a further follow-up from the first group (Volkow et al., 2015) as showing transporter recovery with detoxification, not yet read. A review also argues that repeat-testing artefact is unlikely to explain the PET rise, which balances the statement's emphasis on the missing rescanned controls.
findings.evidence: kish_2017 Dopamine Transporter › Methamphetamine users: Why?, 2nd paragraph (see also Chou et al., 2007; Volkow et al., 2015); ashok_2017 Discussion › Implications (refs 5 and 35) and card sc_ashok_2017 key finding 10; dean_2013 p. 265 (DAT paragraph on Volkow et al., 2001).
findings.proposed: Replace 'The one DAT follow-up with retested controls' with 'A DAT follow-up with retested controls', and add at the end: 'A further follow-up by the first group (Volkow et al., 2015), cited by two reviews as showing transporter recovery with detoxification, has not yet been read. One review judges a repeat-testing artefact unlikely to explain the PET rise (Dean et al., 2013).'

findings.rule: brief B (plain says something the statement and sources do not); source check
findings.issue: The plain says that after long abstinence studies disagree on whether VMAT2 ends up slightly lower. Only one study measured long abstinence (about 10% lower, mean 3.4 years); the normal post-mortem binding result comes from people who had used shortly before death, so it says nothing about long abstinence. The statement does not say when the post-mortem subjects last used.
findings.evidence: kish_2017 Dopamine › Methamphetamine users, 2nd paragraph (all people in the laboratory's post-mortem series, which includes Wilson et al., 1996a, tested positive for methamphetamine or amphetamine at autopsy, within about 5 days of death); VMAT2 › Methamphetamine users, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; hart_2012 p. 593, Table 2.
findings.proposed: plain: replace the last sentence with 'In one scan study of people who had stopped for more than 3 years on average, it was about 10% lower. In brain tissue examined after death, from people who had used meth shortly before dying in one study, it was normal or not clearly lower.' statement: replace 'A review reports post-mortem VMAT2 in people who had used methamphetamine as normal in one binding study' with 'A review reports post-mortem VMAT2 as normal in one binding study of people who had used methamphetamine shortly before death'. Add the kish_2017 anchor 'Dopamine › Methamphetamine users, 2nd paragraph' (as in the dopamine-damage claim, evidence[1]).

findings.rule: brief A (selective use of a number with known reporting problems)
findings.issue: A binding difference of about 10% expressed as g 1.68 implies a between-person SD of only about 6% of the mean, unusual for PET binding; with the review's inconsistent signs, the figure may not be reliable and should not be presented as a 'large standardized difference' without caution.
findings.evidence: kish_2017 VMAT2 section (about 10% lower); ashok_2017 Results › Other dopaminergic measures (g 1.68, 0.86 to 2.5; decreases and increases both positive); card sc_ashok_2017 reporting issue 3.
findings.proposed: Replace 'which a meta-analysis expresses as a large standardized difference (g 1.68)' with 'which a meta-analysis expresses as g 1.68, a value hard to reconcile with a 10% difference unless the spread between people was very small (the review prints VMAT2 decreases and increases with the same sign)'.

findings.rule: brief A (qualifying finding in the same source left out); symmetry
findings.issue: The statement lists the sex imbalance as a confounder but leaves out the paper's separate analyses by sex: the lower relative thalamic and caudate values were reported in both sexes, while the higher whole-brain value was reported only for women (9 vs 6). This weakens the sex-confounding concern for the subcortical result and the reading that those decreases depend on a higher whole-brain value, and it adds a reason to doubt the global excess.
findings.evidence: volkow_2001c p. 386, Results, separate comparisons by sex: women (9 vs 6) higher whole-brain metabolism (t=2.2, df=13) and lower relative thalamus and caudate; men (6 vs 15) lower relative thalamus, caudate and putamen, no whole-brain result given (data not shown). Card sc_volkow_2001c (comparison.matching; reporting issue on p. 386).
findings.proposed: statement: replace 'The two groups also differed in smoking (73% vs 24%) and sex ratio, and cognition was tested only in the methamphetamine group.' with 'The two groups also differed in smoking (73% vs 24%) and in the share of women (60% vs 28%); in separate analyses by sex (9 vs 6 women, 6 vs 15 men; data not shown), the lower relative thalamic and caudate values were reported in both sexes, while the higher whole-brain value was reported only for women. Cognition was tested only in the methamphetamine group.' plain, first sentence: 'One brain-energy study found more activity overall in people who had stopped meth, but the difference did not meet the study's own standard for significance and, when men and women were analysed separately, was reported only for women.' evidence[3].extracted: add 'Separate analyses by sex: women (9 vs 6) higher whole-brain metabolism and lower relative thalamic and caudate metabolism; men (6 vs 15) lower relative thalamic, caudate and putamen metabolism; no whole-brain result given for men.'

findings.rule: brief B and F (internal contradiction)
findings.issue: The statement says metabolism was lower in the thalamus 'only after normalizing', then that thalamic metabolism was about 4% lower in absolute terms; the two halves contradict each other, and the plain repeats the first half.
findings.evidence: statement, 2nd sentence; evidence[6] (absolute thalamus about 4% lower, editors' reading of Figure 2, p. 385).
findings.proposed: statement: replace 'Only after normalizing each region to that higher whole-brain value was metabolism lower in the thalamus (17%) and striatum (6–12%);' with 'Significant decreases appeared only after each region was normalized to that higher whole-brain value (thalamus 17%, striatum 6–12% lower);'. plain: replace 'Deep brain structures looked lower only when compared with that higher overall level.' with 'Deep brain structures looked clearly lower only when compared with that higher overall level; in absolute terms only one of them was slightly lower.'

findings.rule: brief F (overlapping samples across claims)
findings.issue: These are the same 15 people as in the first transporter study (Volkow et al., 2001a), which the paper states; the claim does not, and the two papers give the abstinence range as 35 and 36 months.
findings.evidence: volkow_2001c p. 383, Introduction, last paragraph; p. 384, Participants (2 weeks to 5 months; 11–35 months); volkow_2001a p. 378 (2–24 weeks; 11–36 months).
findings.proposed: 'Adults with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence, abstinent 2 weeks to 35 months (12 of 15 within 5 months; the same 15 people as in the transporter study of Volkow et al., 2001a, which gives the upper limit as 36 months)'.

findings.rule: revision residue (changelog 0.3.4); readable cross-references (changelog 0.3.2)
findings.issue: The reasoning still asserts as fact that these are the same participants as the transporter claim, and uses a claim identifier; statement and plain now call it an inference from matching sample descriptions.
findings.evidence: statement ('apparently the same five… neither paper says so'); wang_2004 p. 243 and volkow_2001b p. 9415 (matching descriptions, no explicit statement).
findings.proposed: 'Observational, starts low. Risk of bias: selected completers, no rescanned controls, statistical reporting errors. Imprecision: five people. Probably the same five people as in the transporter follow-up in section 4 (the editors' inference from matching sample descriptions; neither paper says so), so not independent evidence of recovery.'

findings.rule: brief A (editors' calculation and its assumptions)
findings.issue: The editors' interval for the protracted thalamus comparison (−1.7 to 0.1) assumes the 10 participants named in the Methods; the reported degrees of freedom (df=22) and a later comparison imply 13, with which the interval is about −1.7 to 0.0 (p≈0.05). The card records the ambiguity; the magnitude does not.
findings.evidence: wang_2004 p. 243 (10 in the protracted group), p. 244 (df=22 with 11 controls), p. 245 (N=13); card sc_wang_2004 reporting issue 2.
findings.proposed: '…1.23 vs 1.31 (protracted; reported as not different; editors' calculation d about −0.8, 95% CI −1.7 to 0.1 with the 10 participants named in the Methods, or −1.7 to 0.0 with the 13 implied by the reported degrees of freedom).'

findings.rule: brief B (clarity)
findings.issue: 'Striatal metabolism (+2.7%)' sits in a list beginning 'absolute thalamic metabolism', but +2.7% is the relative (region-to-global) change.
findings.evidence: wang_2004 p. 244, Results, 1st paragraph.
findings.proposed: Replace 'while absolute thalamic metabolism, striatal metabolism (+2.7%) and global metabolism (about −4%, editors' calculation) did not change significantly' with 'while relative striatal metabolism (+2.7%), absolute regional metabolism and global metabolism (about −4%, editors' calculation) did not change significantly'.

findings.rule: METHODS §5.3 (the instrument must match the design; narrative reviews use the editors' checklist and are never primary evidence)
findings.issue: The cited card is designed as a narrative review but appraised with AMSTAR 2 (overall critically low), which §5.3 reserves for systematic reviews; the four other narrative reviews this claim cites use the editors' checklist. The debate then cites this review alone for an empirical statement about animals.
findings.evidence: Card sc_kish_2008: design 'narrative-review', risk_of_bias.instrument 'AMSTAR 2'; sample.recruitment (no search or selection method); selection_effects (human dopamine evidence cited only to the author's own study). Cards sc_hart_2012, sc_dean_2013, sc_kish_2017, sc_london_2015 use the checklist.
findings.proposed: Re-appraise sc_kish_2008 with the editors' narrative-review checklist (suggested from the card's own notes, for the readers to confirm: systematic search and explicit selection high; appraisal of cited studies high; reliance on the author's own work high; separation of evidence from speculation some concerns; balance some concerns; overall high) and rerun scripts/rob_vocab.py. In debate.evidence_yes write 'In animals, high doses damage striatal dopamine terminals (as summarized in a narrative review, Kish, 2008)'.

findings.rule: brief F (claims that contradict each other)
findings.issue: The statement, plain and editors' reading speak of one small follow-up in which the transporter rose, but the transporter-recovery claim in the same section reports a second (SPECT, 5 people, mean 20% rise over 2 weeks, 7 retested controls), and two cited reviews point to a third from the first group (Volkow et al., 2015, not yet read) as showing recovery with detoxification.
findings.evidence: cl_meth_dat_recovery statement and evidence[8] (dean_2013 p. 265, Chou et al., 2007); kish_2017 Dopamine Transporter › Methamphetamine users: Why?, 2nd paragraph; ashok_2017 Discussion › Implications (refs 5, 35).
findings.proposed: statement: replace 'in one small follow-up the transporter rose with abstinence, while cross-sectional studies found no relation with time since last use' with 'in two small follow-ups of five people each the transporter rose with abstinence (over about 14 months, and over 2 weeks from a first scan taken while urine tests were still positive), while cross-sectional studies found no relation with time since last use; a third follow-up (Volkow et al., 2015), cited by two reviews as showing recovery, has not been read'. plain: replace 'and in one small follow-up the transporter rose again after people stopped, though other studies found no such pattern' with 'and in two small follow-ups the transporter rose again after people stopped, though studies comparing people with different times since last use found no such link'. editors_reading: replace 'one follow-up of five selected people found a rise' with 'two small follow-ups found a rise (five people selected by staying abstinent for about 14 months; five people over 2 weeks, first scanned while urine tests were still positive)'. evidence_no: after the first sentence add 'A SPECT follow-up of five people found a mean 20% rise over 2 weeks, though the first scan was taken while urine tests were still positive (Chou et al., 2007, as described by Dean et al., 2013).', with the dean_2013 p. 265 anchor used in the recovery claim.

findings.rule: source check (anchor at the stated place)
findings.issue: The marker-confound argument and the statement that structural terminal damage has not been examined post-mortem are in the 3rd paragraph of the Conclusions; the 2nd is the authors' speculation paragraph. The card's second reader already corrected the same locator; the claim was not updated.
findings.evidence: kish_2017 Conclusions: 1st paragraph (premature to conclude), 2nd (speculation on depletion and down-regulation), 3rd (marker confound; no post-mortem structural studies in people who used methamphetamine). Card sc_kish_2017 verification.disagreements.
findings.proposed: 'Conclusions, 3rd paragraph'.

findings.rule: METHODS §7 (each side at its best proponents' standard); brief A
findings.issue: The 'yes' side omits that two of the 20 people in the post-mortem series had near-total (95% and 97%) caudate dopamine loss, which the authors place in the 'Parkinsonian range'; the card's second reader flagged this as qualifying the claim. The first imaging group also states that three people had transporter levels within the range of mild Parkinson's disease (values not shown).
findings.evidence: kish_2017 Comment › 'Marked dopamine loss in some methamphetamine users could be harmful', 2nd paragraph; card sc_kish_2017 key findings and verification.disagreements; volkow_2001a p. 380, Discussion; card sc_volkow_2001a reporting issue 4.
findings.proposed: evidence_yes: after 'in one laboratory's series not yet independently replicated (Kish et al., 2017)' insert '; two of the 20 had near-total (95% and 97%) caudate dopamine loss, a level the authors place in the Parkinsonian range, and the first imaging group reports that three people had transporter levels within the range of mild Parkinson's disease, without showing the values (Volkow, Chang, Wang, Fowler, Leonido-Yee, et al., 2001)'. New anchor: reference kish_2017, locator 'Comment › Marked dopamine loss in some methamphetamine users…, 2nd paragraph', extracted 'Two people in the post-mortem series had 95% and 97% caudate dopamine loss, placed by the authors in the Parkinsonian range; the authors think these two probably had some behavioural impairment.', role 'qualifies'.

findings.rule: METHODS §4.4 (each citation exposes its anchors); brief A (wording no stronger than the source)
findings.issue: The 'no' side cites Dean et al. (2013) for rat pre-exposure, but no Dean anchor is attached to this claim, and 'prevented the effects' overstates both sources: Hart says the changes can be prevented, Dean that escalating pre-exposure attenuated binge deficits and, in a few studies, largely prevented cognitive deficits.
findings.evidence: dean_2013 p. 260, Hypothesis 1, 4th paragraph (Segal et al., 2003; Belcher et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2007; Simoes et al., 2007); hart_2012 p. 589.
findings.proposed: evidence_no: replace 'and in a few rat studies escalating pre-exposure prevented the effects of a later binge (Hart et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2013)' with 'and in a few rat studies escalating pre-exposure attenuated the neurobiological and behavioural effects of a later binge (Hart et al., 2012) and largely prevented its cognitive effects (Dean et al., 2013)'. New anchor: reference dean_2013, page 'p. 260', locator 'Hypothesis 1, 4th paragraph', extracted 'An escalating regimen in rats attenuated behavioural and biological deficits from later binge doses (Segal et al., 2003), and in a few studies largely prevented binge-induced object-recognition and working-memory deficits.', role 'qualifies'.

findings.rule: brief A (qualifying finding in the same source); brief E (translation from animals)
findings.issue: The 'yes' side states as fact that the vervet-monkey regimen is closer to human use (the reviewers' description) and that transporter and D2-type availability fell, without noting that no magnitudes are given and that the same review reports D2-type availability recovering with protracted abstinence in nonhuman primates, which bears on whether the change indicates damage.
findings.evidence: london_2015 Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 6th paragraph and Figure 2 legend; Molecular Imaging of Methamphetamine Users › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph (D2-type availability recovers with protracted abstinence in rodents and nonhuman primates, Groman et al., 2012; no human longitudinal D2 studies); dean_2013 p. 260 (the monkeys' deficits improved with abstinence).
findings.proposed: evidence_yes: replace 'and monkeys given an escalating regimen, closer to human use, had lower transporter and D2-type receptor availability (London et al., 2015)' with 'and in vervet monkeys given an escalating regimen that reviewers describe as resembling human use, transporter and D2-type receptor availability fell (London et al., 2015; magnitudes not reported)'. evidence_no: add 'In the same monkey model, D2-type receptor availability recovered with protracted abstinence (Groman et al., 2012, as summarized by London et al., 2015).' New anchor: reference london_2015, locator 'Molecular Imaging of Methamphetamine Users › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph', extracted 'Striatal D2-type receptor availability is reported to recover with protracted abstinence in rodents and nonhuman primates (Groman et al., 2012); no longitudinal human D2 studies.', role 'qualifies'.

findings.rule: METHODS §9 (person-first language)
findings.issue: The displayed reasoning says 'post-mortem users'.
findings.evidence: grade.reasoning, 2nd sentence.
findings.proposed: 'Observational and post-mortem evidence, starts low. Risk of bias: the people examined post-mortem had used shortly before death, so acute depletion and lasting damage are confounded; imaging samples are small and selected. Indirectness: the markers are surrogates for neuron or terminal loss, and the animal evidence uses regimens unlike human use.'

findings.rule: brief F (same fact worded differently across claims)
findings.issue: 'VMAT2 … normal post-mortem' is firmer than the VMAT2 claim (normal in one study, not significantly different with a trend lower in another) and omits that the binding study was of people who had used shortly before death.
findings.evidence: cl_meth_vmat2 statement; kish_2017 VMAT2 section and Dopamine › Methamphetamine users, 2nd paragraph.

findings.rule: brief B (plain differs from the statement)
findings.issue: The plain attributes both the smaller and the larger regions to scans in the first week after stopping; in the statement and the review, the larger striatal and parietal volumes come from people abstinent 3–4 months on average or still using. It also drops the uncorrected threshold of the one-month increase.
findings.evidence: statement; london_2015 Structural Brain Imaging, 2nd paragraph (Jernigan et al., 2005; Chang et al., 2005; Jan et al., 2012); dean_2013 p. 266, Figure 1 note (uncorrected threshold).
findings.proposed: 'Brain scans taken about a week after stopping showed some regions with less grey matter (differences of up to about 11% in one study) in people dependent on meth. Other studies, of people who had stopped for 3–4 months on average or were still using, found some regions larger. Most people who use meth also smoke tobacco, and in the study that checked, smokers who don't use meth showed some of the same differences. People who used meth also had less schooling and more symptoms of depression. In one study, grey matter grew in several regions over the first month without meth, though by a lenient statistical standard. An early finding of a smaller memory region (the hippocampus) was not repeated by the same lab.'

findings.rule: brief A (selective use of a source)
findings.issue: Against non-smoking controls, the study that separated smoking found smaller grey matter in the left caudate and right precuneus as well as in frontal, cingulate, insular and temporal regions; the statement lists only the latter and then reports larger striatal and parietal volumes elsewhere, hiding that the studies disagree in exactly those regions. The review also says smokers without methamphetamine use had smaller caudate as well as orbitofrontal grey matter.
findings.evidence: Anchor 8 (Morales et al., 2012, Table 2: the ten clusters include left caudate and right precuneus); london_2015 Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 4th paragraph (smokers with and without methamphetamine use had smaller OFC and caudate than non-smokers; possibly smoking or pre-morbid); card sc_morales_2012 key finding 4 (supplementary caudate analysis, supplement unread).
findings.proposed: statement, first sentence: replace 'less grey matter in some frontal, cingulate, insular and temporal regions' with 'less grey matter in some frontal, cingulate, insular, temporal and parietal (precuneus) regions and in the left caudate'. Smoking sentence: replace 'non-using smokers also had less orbitofrontal grey matter than non-smokers' with 'non-using smokers also had less orbitofrontal grey matter than non-smokers (and, in a supplementary analysis described by a review, less caudate grey matter)'. New anchor: reference london_2015, locator 'Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 4th paragraph', extracted 'Smokers with and without methamphetamine use had smaller OFC and caudate grey matter than non-smokers (Morales et al., 2012); the reviewers suggest these deficits may partly reflect smoking or pre-morbid conditions.', role 'qualifies'.

findings.rule: brief A (population as studied)
findings.issue: 'Both studies read scanned people in their first week' fits the verified 4–7 days in one study; in the other, abstinence was a self-reported mean of 6.6 days (SD 5.2), unverified, and a review groups it with brief abstinence under 3 weeks.
findings.evidence: card sc_thompson_2004 exposure.abstinence_at_testing (Table 3); card sc_morales_2012 (Methods §2.1); london_2015 Structural Brain Imaging, 2nd paragraph.
findings.proposed: Replace 'Both studies read scanned people in their first week without methamphetamine;' with 'Both studies read scanned people about a week after last use on average (4–7 days, verified by urine tests, in one; a self-reported mean of 6.6 days, SD 5.2, in the other);'.

findings.rule: brief A and symmetry (finding in the same source left out)

summary: The eleven claims are carefully hedged and their numbers almost all reproduce at the stated places: 79 of the 82 anchors from saved sources were confirmed (5 with caveats), and every GRADE calculation is arithmetically correct. The serious problems are misreadings introduced or left behind in revision: the transporter claim applies the meta-analysis's '5 days to 3 weeks' abstinence (which describes all 31 studies) to the nine transporter studies, three of which had groups abstinent for years; the VMAT2 plain text treats post-mortem data from people who used shortly before death as evidence about long abstinence; and the dopamine-damage claim speaks of one follow-up where the monograph documents two (a third, Volkow et al., 2015, is unread). Several qualifiers that the cards already record, some favouring and some cutting against the claims, have not reached the statements: the sex-stratified metabolism analysis, Sekine's sample without other drug use, near-total caudate dopamine loss in 2 of 20 post-mortem cases, the liberal 16th-percentile impairment cut-off, the 71% exclusion that shaped the Utah cohort, and the recovery of D2-type binding in the monkey model. Some anchors, domain notes and reasoning texts no longer match revised statements (a missing Johanson anchor, the uncorrected '−0.65', 'same participants', 'one other PET study', 'users').
